framing: The trick that makes billion-parameter models possible
paragraphs: Chapter 1 trained a model by nudging each knob and checking whether the loss improved. That works for two knobs. For a billion, one training step would take a billion passes over the data, and training would never finish. A language model only exists because there is a much cheaper way to get the same answer.

The method is called backpropagation, and it needs very little mathematics: one rule about how rates combine, plus a few simple derivatives. You will not be asked to prove anything. You will be asked to follow some numbers through a small calculation, which you can do with a finger on the page.

We will begin with a single knob and learn what a slope tells you and what it does not, including how a correct gradient can still destroy a training run. Then we will see why straight lines are not enough, build the smallest possible neural network, and run a backward pass on it by hand.

When you finish, the backward call in PyTorch will no longer be magic. You will know what it computes and what memory it needs. You will also know how too large a learning rate turns a training log to NaN, and the three ways gradients commonly go wrong, most of which raise no error at all.
outcomes: Compute a derivative with the chain rule and use it for a gradient descent step.
Explain why neural networks need nonlinearities, and what a learning rate that is too large does.
Carry out a backward pass by hand and verify it with a gradient check.
question: If a model has a billion parameters, why does computing all of their gradients cost about as much as one extra pass through the model?
